title: A white SUV crossing a signalised junction (Caton Farm Road / Essington Road, Joliet, Illinois, 22 Aug 2026)
author: Illinois_Roadbuff (Rogue Jr), via Wikimedia Commons
attribution: Views of the Caton Farm Road and Essington Road Intersection in Joliet, Illinois, by Illinois_Roadbuff (Rogue Jr), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Trimmed (0.0-4.4 s of the first fixed-camera segment), audio removed, scaled from 4096x2160 (non-square pixels, 15:16) to 1280x720 and re-encoded.

trimmed_from.source_frames: first 4.4 s of the file (about 264 frames at 59.94 fps)

scale_hints.object: The white SUV itself: looks like a GMC Acadia (second generation, 2017-2023), bumper to bumper about 4.9 m. Identified by eye from the shape and tail-lights, NOT confirmed, so treat as an estimate; any mid-size SUV is 4.7-5.0 m.
scale_hints.source: Estimate (GMC Acadia 2017-2019 is about 193.6 in = 4.92 m per the manufacturer's spec; verify, and the model may be wrong). About 610 px long at 2.4 s in the 1280x720 frame.

question: How fast is this car going, in km/h?
notes: Source: a 131 s, 4K, 59.94 fps tripod-mounted compilation of an intersection; this is the first segment (0-59 s), one fixed shot (pole, signal head and wires stay put; at most a few px of drift). Not a school street: a four-lane signalised junction in the US, so the vehicle is turning or pulling away on a green and is probably slow (by eye roughly 15-25 km/h; this is NOT a measurement). A '30' sign is visible beyond the pole (probably 30 mph; not verified). Timeline: the SUV's front appears at the left edge at about 0.55 s (frame ~33), the whole car is in shot from about 1.4 s, it moves left to right, passes behind the grey signal pole (x about 1000-1060 px) at about 3.0-3.6 s and is gone by about 3.8 s (frame ~228); a dark SUV enters at the left edge at about 4.0 s, so it is not in the trimmed clip except for a sliver at the very end. Length in frame: about 610 px (bumper to bumper) at 2.4 s, shrinking to about 545 px by 3.0 s because the car recedes slightly (the road runs away to the right), so the scale is NOT constant: perspective is oblique, not purely side-on, and the car is rotated slightly toward the camera at the start. Scale references: the SUV (about 4.9 m, estimate); the white zebra crosswalk bars behind it (US ladder bars, nominal 0.3-0.6 m wide, spacing 0.6-1.2 m; unverified); the 30 sign. The frame has thin black letterbox bars at top and bottom (about 22 px). Plates: the rear plate faces the camera at the start but is about 20 px wide and not legible; the windows are tinted and the driver is not identifiable. No people are visible in the clip. Other cars in the distance are tiny. Licence: CC BY 4.0, so keep the credit.

title: John Young's jump salute on the Moon (Apollo 16, 21 Apr 1972)
author: NASA (Apollo 16 rover TV camera; clip prepared by Ken Glover for the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)
licence: Public domain (NASA work; ALSJ video clips)
attribution: Apollo 16 rover TV, John Young's Big Navy Salute. NASA / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, public domain; trimmed, upscaled 2x and re-encoded.

scale_hints.object: Astronaut in the A7L suit with PLSS, standing height (the jumper is about 1.8 m tall in the suit)
scale_hints.source: John Young was 5 ft 9 in (1.75 m) tall; the suit and backpack add little standing height. Approximate: check against ALSJ/NASA biography.

expected.meaning: lunar surface gravity (the jump gives a smaller-than-Earth value; the fit will be rough because of the 1972 TV resolution)

question: John Young jumps and salutes. What is the gravity on the Moon?
notes: Apollo 16 EVA-1, 21 Apr 1972, rover TV camera parked near the flag; Young is the large figure in front (about 270 px tall in the 704x480 clip, seen from behind and slightly side-on), Duke is the small figure by the flag. Camera still throughout the trimmed clip (flag and horizon fixed). Take-off about frame 29 (0.97 s), peak about frame 49, landing about frame 69 (2.3 s), so roughly 1.3 s in the air; clip runs 0-3.37 s (101 frames at 29.97 fps). Original is 352x240 at 29.97 fps, upscaled 2x by us. No exact duplicate frames in the trimmed range, but the frame differences dip every fifth frame, a sign the TV copy was converted from a 24 fps source (film or a 24-to-30 conversion): effective sampling may be about 24 fps with blended frames, so expect timing jitter of up to one frame. Back-lit by the sun: the astronaut's legs can be dark. Young also waves/salutes with his right arm during the jump.

expected.meaning: net upward acceleration at liftoff (fitted g is negative: the rocket accelerates up)
expected.source: NASA: 8.8 Mlbf (39.1 MN) liftoff thrust, 5.75 Mlb (2.61 Mkg) liftoff mass; thrust/weight 1.53, so a = 0.53 g = 5.2 m/s²

question: How hard does the rocket accelerate off the pad?
notes: Fixed pad camera at night. The base is below the frame and the lower rocket vanishes into exhaust glare, so the nose (top edge) is the clean point to track. Expected values are approximate: thrust ramps at ignition.
